newsitem.title: USA: Amoco U.S. sale signals move overseas.
newsitem.headline: Amoco U.S. sale signals move overseas.

text.p: Amoco Corp's planned sale of 15 percent of its U.S. reserves could fetch $2.0-$2.5 billion and signals a move overseas, where oil majors believe big reserve additions can be achieved.

Amoco said the assets to be sold represented 10 percent of domestic production in 1996 and one-third of its working interest properties. The assets are located in Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico, Oklahoma and the Gulf Coast.
Amoco did not dislose a price for the proposed sale but analysts said the deal could be worth $2.0-$2.5 billion.

"We are becoming more international, our strategy is to enter into proven reserves overseas -- in Venezuela, Trinidad, the Nile Delta and the Caspian Sea as well as offshore Gulf of Mexico," said Amoco spokesman Jim Spangler.
In 1996 Amoco replaced 169 percent of production globally and 435 percent of overseas production, reflecting a greater emphasis on its overseas operations.

"Amoco reached a decision that the highest return on its invested capital was not going to be in the U.S., and they are finally putting their money where their mouth is," said Fadel Gheit, analyst at Fahenstock & Co.
Amoco shares rose 5/8 to 90 following the company's announcement Monday morning.
Amoco's total reserves at the end of 1996 were 5.8 billion barrels of oil equivalent. It produced 483 million barrels of oil equivalent in the year.
The company has already combined its Permian Basin, Texas, and southeast New Mexico oil and gas assets with Shell Oil Co, a unit of Royal Dutch/Shell.
It also plans to create a small joint venture to produce natural gas in the U.S. midcontinent with Maxus Energy, a subsidiary of Argentine oil company YPF SA.

Analysts say most of the Amoco assets to be sold produce natural gas. Potential buyers include Burlington Resources Inc and Union Pacific Resources Inc, both of which have large cash balances and the ability to borrow, analysts said.
"The independents can operate these sorts of fields far more efficiently than the majors. We will probably see some assets sold on to a third party," said Fahenstock's Gheit.

The Amoco deal is the latest in a series of mergers and acquisitions in the upstream oil and gas industry, on Friday DuPont Co's Conoco unit announced a $900 million deal to buy assets in south Texas.

Amoco has already signaled, with its $2.0 billion share buyback and a 7.5 percent increase in its dividend, that it is focused on improving shareholder value. The sale of the U.S. properties and its overseas focus confirm that trend, analysts said.

The company said its most significant reserve additions in 1996 came from its discovery of eight trillion cubic feet of natural gas in Trinidad. Its 17 percent interest in three working oilfields in the Azerbaijani Caspian Sea added 69 million barrels to reserves.
The company prequalified for the latest bidding for oil reserves in Venezuela, where it already has substantial interests.
